\section[o engarrafamento]{o engarrafamento — the traffic jam}

\label{lesson:PT-C409-engarrafamento}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the speed camera, then the Portuguese for to inspect.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o engarrafamento}
\textbf{o engarrafamento} — \textquotedblleft{}the traffic jam\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ficámos uma hora no engarrafamento.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{We were stuck in the traffic jam for an hour.}
\end{quote}

Literally a 'bottling'. In Brazil also \emph{o congestionamento}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{engarrafamento} is built on \emph{engarrafar} 'to bottle, to put in a bottle' with \emph{-mento} (EtymDB): traffic squeezed as if through a bottleneck.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o engarrafamento}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o engarrafamento}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{o engarrafamento}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the speed camera, then the Portuguese for to inspect, then say \emph{o engarrafamento} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does o engarrafamento mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The traffic jam\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[abrandar]{abrandar — to slow down}

\label{lesson:PT-C409-abrandar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to inspect, then the Portuguese for the traffic jam.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: abrandar}
\textbf{abrandar} — \textquotedblleft{}to slow down\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Os carros abrandam perto da escola.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The cars slow down near the school.}
\end{quote}

Also of rain or wind: \emph{a chuva abrandou}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{abrandar} is built from \emph{a-}, \emph{brando} 'soft, gentle' and \emph{-ar} (EtymDB); \emph{brando} is inherited from Latin \emph{blandus} 'gentle, pleasant'.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{abrandar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{abrandar}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{abrandar}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to inspect, then the Portuguese for the traffic jam, then say \emph{abrandar} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does abrandar mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To slow down\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[a colisão]{a colisão — the collision}

\label{lesson:PT-C409-colisao}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the traffic jam, then the Portuguese for to slow down.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: a colisão}
\textbf{a colisão} — \textquotedblleft{}the collision\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Houve uma colisão entre dois carros na ponte.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There was a collision between two cars on the bridge.}
\end{quote}

A formal word, common in the news.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{colisão} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{collīsiō} (EtymDB), from \emph{collīdere} 'to strike together' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the traffic jam, then the Portuguese for to slow down, then say \emph{a colisão} again

\section[embater]{embater — to crash into, to hit}

\label{lesson:PT-C409-embater}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to slow down, then the Portuguese for the collision.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: embater}
\textbf{embater} — \textquotedblleft{}to crash into, to hit\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A mota embateu num carro parado.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The motorbike crashed into a parked car.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Embater em} — to crash into.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{embater} is built from \emph{em-} and \emph{bater} 'to hit', which is inherited from Late Latin \emph{battere}, Latin \emph{battuere} 'to beat' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[o desvio]{o desvio — the diversion, the detour}

\label{lesson:PT-C409-desvio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the collision, then the Portuguese for to crash into.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o desvio}
\textbf{o desvio} — \textquotedblleft{}the diversion, the detour\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Por causa das obras, há um desvio pela aldeia.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Because of the roadworks, there is a diversion through the village.}
\end{quote}

The verb is \emph{desviar}, to divert or to turn aside.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{desvio} is built on \emph{desviar} 'to turn aside', which is inherited from Latin \emph{dēviāre}, on \emph{via} 'way' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o desvio}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o desvio}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{o desvio}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the collision, then the Portuguese for to crash into, then say \emph{o desvio} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does o desvio mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The diversion, the detour\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
